subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following is a naturally occurring modelling material traditionally used for 3D work?
options: Polystyrene
Clay
Acrylic sheet
MDF
questions.explain: Clay is a natural earth-based material widely used for modelling and ceramic 3D work.

questions.q: In ceramics, what is the term for clay that has been fired once but not yet glazed?
options: Greenware
Bisque (biscuit) ware
Slipware
Leather-hard clay
questions.explain: Bisque, or biscuit, ware is clay that has undergone a first firing but remains unglazed and porous.

questions.q: Why is a maquette often made before producing a large 3D sculpture?
options: To replace the final piece entirely
To test form, scale and proportion on a small, low-cost scale
Because large materials cannot be sourced
To avoid drawing the design first
questions.explain: A maquette is a small preliminary model that lets an artist trial form, scale and structure before committing to the full-size work.

questions.q: Which process involves pouring a liquid material into a mould to take on its shape once set?
options: Casting
Carving
Weaving
Etching
questions.explain: Casting fills a mould with a liquid such as molten metal or plaster that hardens into the mould's form.

questions.q: What is the main difference between an additive and a subtractive 3D process?
options: Additive removes material; subtractive builds it up
Additive builds form by adding material; subtractive removes material to reveal form
Both remove material but at different speeds
They are two names for the same technique
questions.explain: Additive processes such as modelling add material, whereas subtractive processes such as carving cut material away.

questions.q: A student wants to create a solid figure by cutting and chiselling away from a single block of soap. Which process are they using?
options: Modelling
Carving (subtractive)
Casting
Construction
questions.explain: Cutting material away from a solid block is carving, a subtractive process.

questions.q: Why might an artist choose plaster rather than clay for a particular 3D study?
options: Plaster can never be carved
Plaster sets quickly and can be both cast and carved once hardened
Plaster is always stronger than any metal
Plaster cannot be moulded at all
questions.explain: Plaster is versatile: it can be cast in a mould and then carved or refined once set.

questions.q: In 3D design, what does the term 'form' describe?
options: A flat, two-dimensional outline
A three-dimensional shape that has height, width and depth
The surface colour of an object
The texture of a surface only
questions.explain: Form refers to a shape existing in three dimensions, possessing height, width and depth.

questions.q: What is meant by 'negative space' in a 3D sculpture?
options: The solid mass of the object
The empty space around and through the form
The base the sculpture stands on
The shadow cast by the piece
questions.explain: Negative space is the empty area surrounding and passing through a form, which shapes how the solid mass is read.

questions.q: Why is viewing a sculpture 'in the round' important?
options: It has only one intended viewpoint
It is designed to be seen and understood from all angles
It should be viewed only from the front
It must always be viewed from above
questions.explain: A sculpture in the round is freestanding and intended to be experienced from every viewpoint.

questions.q: A relief sculpture is best described as one that is:
options: Fully freestanding and viewable from all sides
Projecting from, but attached to, a flat background surface
Made only from woven fibres
Always life-sized
questions.explain: Relief work projects from a background plane rather than standing free in the round.

questions.q: A designer wants a tall model to stay upright without toppling. Which structural principle should they prioritise?
options: A narrow, high centre of gravity
A stable, wide base and balanced distribution of weight
Placing all weight at the very top
Removing the base entirely
questions.explain: A wide base and low, balanced centre of gravity give a tall structure stability.

questions.q: How can scale affect the impact of a 3D piece?
options: Scale has no effect on how a piece is perceived
A dramatic change in scale can alter mood, presence and the viewer's response
Only colour affects impact, not scale
Larger always means lower quality
questions.explain: Altering scale can make a form feel monumental or intimate, changing how a viewer responds to it.

questions.q: In hand-building with clay, what is the 'coiling' technique?
options: Rolling clay into ropes and stacking them to build walls
Pressing clay into a plaster mould
Spinning clay on a wheel
Cutting flat slabs and joining them
questions.explain: Coiling builds vessel walls by layering and joining rolled ropes of clay.

questions.q: When joining two pieces of leather-hard clay, what is applied at the join for a secure bond?
options: Slip and scored (scratched) surfaces
Dry powder only
Varnish
Wax
questions.explain: Scoring the surfaces and adding slip (liquid clay) creates a strong join between clay pieces.

questions.q: Why is an armature often used when modelling with a soft material such as clay or wax?
options: To add surface colour
To provide an internal supporting framework that holds the form's shape
To fire the piece more quickly
To make the piece heavier
questions.explain: An armature is an internal skeleton that supports soft material and stops the modelled form from collapsing.

questions.q: A student is assembling a model from card, wire and found objects glued and slotted together. Which construction method is this?
options: Carving
Casting
Assemblage / construction from parts
Throwing on a wheel
questions.explain: Building a form by joining separate components together is assemblage, a constructive technique.

questions.q: Why should hollow clay forms have a small hole or be made thin-walled before firing?
options: To make them lighter to carry only
To allow trapped air and moisture to escape so the piece does not crack or explode in the kiln
To add decoration
To help the glaze stick
questions.explain: Trapped air or moisture expands during firing, so venting hollow forms prevents cracking or bursting in the kiln.

questions.q: The slab-building technique in ceramics involves:
options: Rolling clay into flat sheets that are cut and joined
Stacking rolled coils
Pinching a ball of clay outwards
Pouring liquid clay into a mould
questions.explain: Slab building uses flat rolled sheets of clay cut to shape and joined together to form the object.

questions.q: A student wants a symmetrical, round pot with smooth even walls. Which making technique is most suitable?
options: Throwing on a potter's wheel
Random assemblage of found parts
Carving from a solid block
Flat collage
questions.explain: Throwing on a wheel uses rotation to produce symmetrical, round forms with even walls.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Art & Design (0400) syllabus; Three-Dimensional Design
